extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and applicants (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (as amended by AIPA and the CREATE Act) in prosecution, reexamination, and reissue — including when prior art may be disqualified due to common ownership or joint research agreements and what evidence is required. Focuses on timing, scope, proofs, and procedural requirements for establishing disqualification of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability/effective-dates of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (AIPA/CREATE Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CREATE Act amendments to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) apply to patents granted on or after December 10, 2004 (except patents subject to the current 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103); the 1999 AIPA changes apply to applications filed on or after November 29, 1999. For reexamination, look to the patent grant date and whether the patent is subject to the current 35 U.S.C. 102/103 to determine which version applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining which statutory version applies, consider filing date, grant date, whether application/patent is subject to current 102/103, and whether action/court decisions predate Dec 10, 2004. Reissue and reexamination have special considerations; consult MPEP §§ 2159, 2146.01 and Office legal administration when recapture issues arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of disqualified prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) disqualifies only subject matter that qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g) and is being relied upon in a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 103(c) cannot be used to disqualify references relied on for anticipation under 102; anticipatory 102 rejections remain available. 103(c) also cannot be used to overcome or prevent double patenting rejections; double patenting rejections should still be made as appropriate (see 37 CFR 1.78(c) and MPEP § 804).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership requirement — complete/100% ownership at time invention was made
rubrics_metrics.description: To disqualify a reference under pre-AIA 103(c) via common ownership, the subject matter (reference) and the claimed invention must have been entirely/wholly owned by, or subject to an obligation to assign to, the same person(s) or entity(ies) at the time the claimed invention was made. Ownership less than 100% defeats common ownership for this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application is co-owned by multiple entities, the reference must have been co-owned by that same set of entities (or subject to the same obligation to assign) on the date the later invention was made. A mere present statement of common ownership is insufficient; ownership must have existed at the time of invention. Licenses that retain basic ownership rights generally do not defeat common ownership. Examples and multi-entity scenarios are provided (joint ventures, subsidiaries, percentage ownership illustrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of ownership/invention — 'at the time the invention was made' / conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ownership (or a joint research agreement) must have existed on or before the date the claimed invention was made (i.e., when conception was complete). Ownership obtained after the invention date cannot be used to disqualify prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invention timing follows case law (e.g., Mergenthaler, In re Tansel, Pfaff v. Wells Electronics) — invention is 'made' when conception is complete and the invention is ready for patenting (e.g., sufficient drawings or descriptions). Examine facts to determine whether ownership or JRA was in effect on that date; foreign/foreign filing issues noted (pre-AIA 104 interplay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — applicant/patentee must establish disqualification once examiner makes prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an examiner establishes a prima facie case of obviousness under pre-AIA 103(a) based on a reference, the burden to establish that the subject matter is disqualified as prior art under pre-AIA 103(c) rests on the person asserting disqualification (typically the applicant or patentee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are expected to provide the necessary statement or objective evidence; examiners will assume compliance with duty of disclosure unless evidence suggests otherwise. Placing the burden on the examiner or litigation defendant is inappropriate because relevant evidence is often within the applicant/patentee’s control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient statement of common ownership (form and signature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear and conspicuous signed statement that the application and the reference 'were, at the time the invention was made, owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person' is sufficient to establish common ownership for pre-AIA 103(c) purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be prominent (e.g., on a separate paper) and signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). Example wording is provided in the MPEP. Applicants may but are not required to submit additional evidence (assignments, affidavits, court decisions). If no contrary evidence exists, the statement alone disqualifies the reference for a 103(a) rejection based on 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence that may be submitted to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence that may be submitted includes: (A) recorded assignments in the USPTO conveying entire rights to the same person(s)/organization(s); (B) copies of unrecorded assignments conveying entire rights and filed in the applications; (C) an affidavit or declaration by the common owner stating facts explaining why common ownership exists and properly signed; and (D) other evidence establishing common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the signed statement is often sufficient, applicants can submit any of the listed objective proofs to bolster or substantiate the declaration. Affidavits/declarations should be by an authorized official and explain facts supporting ownership. Examiners may request such evidence when there is material doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's authority to question representations and require objective evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner has independent evidence raising a material doubt about the accuracy of an applicant’s representation of common ownership or obligation to assign, the examiner may explain the doubt and require objective evidence of common ownership (e.g., assignments, affidavits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should identify why the representation is doubted. Note that execution dates on assignment documents may not reflect the date a party was under an obligation to assign; examiners should consider substance over form. If objective evidence is required, the examiner must state the basis for the doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and statutory requirements for 'joint research agreement' under pre-AIA 103(c) (CREATE Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: For pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended by the CREATE Act, a 'joint research agreement' is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. To qualify, (A) the claimed invention must have been made by or on behalf of the parties to the JRA that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention must result from activities within the scope of the JRA; and (C) the patent application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The JRA need only be in effect on or before the date the later invention was made (not required to be in effect on or before the prior art date). The applicant must comply with the statute and rules of practice (including disclosure). The burden to prove JRA applicability rests on applicant once prima facie obviousness is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements to disclose parties to a joint research agreement (37 CFR 1.71(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification may disclose or be amended to disclose the names of parties to a joint research agreement per 37 CFR 1.71(g). An amendment to disclose must be accompanied by the processing fee (per § 1.17(i)) unless filed within certain time windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time windows where no processing fee is required: within three months of filing date of a national application; within three months of national stage entry; before mailing of a first Office action on the merits; or before mailing of a first Office action after filing a RCE under § 1.114. If amendment is after issue fee paid and the patent as issued doesn’t include the names, a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and § 1.323 is needed for the amendment to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on reissue and recapture doctrine considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The recapture doctrine may prevent presentation of claims in a reissue that were amended or canceled to overcome a 103(a) rejection based on prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) that could not be disqualified under 103(c) during original prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner determines recapture may apply in a reissue, consultation with the Office of Patent Legal Administration via the Technology Center Quality Assurance Specialist should be initiated. CREATE Act timing and prior prosecution history must be considered when evaluating reissue claims and disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory treatment under 37 CFR 1.104(c)(5) for statements of common ownership or JRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 CFR 1.104(c)(5), subject matter qualifying as prior art under pre-March 16, 2013 102(e),(f),(g) and a claimed invention in certain applications or patents will be treated as commonly owned for purposes of pre-AIA 103(c) if the applicant/patent owner provides the required statement. Similarly, JRA-based treatment is available if the applicant provides a statement that the subject matter and claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a qualifying JRA and the application discloses the names of the JRA parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulatory provision parallels statutory requirements and sets out the circumstances and filing/patent dates where a statement will be treated as establishing common ownership or JRA basis. Follow the regulatory text for which applications/patents and dates are covered (e.g., filed on/after Nov 29, 1999; pending on/after Dec 10, 2004; patents granted on/after Dec 10, 2004).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples and fact patterns for establishing common ownership/JRA
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP provides multiple concrete examples (subsidiaries, percentage ownership splits, joint ventures, university-company JRAs, spinoffs) showing when inventions are or are not commonly owned or when an obligation to assign establishes common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate application of the 100% ownership rule, how obligations to assign flow (e.g., employee obligations to university which in turn has obligation to joint venture), that present ownership after invention does not suffice, and that statements on file can establish common ownership absent contradictory evidence. Use examples to analogize to factual situations and to determine sufficiency of a statement or need for objective evidence.
